Hypergraph PageRank: where the interaction flow spends its time

honets

2026-08-25

The analytic question

The windowed-hyperedge tutorial established which action combinations recur in the human_long pair-programming sessions and which actions anchor them structurally (H-eigenvector centrality). This tutorial asks a different question: if session activity is treated as a flow that wanders from action to action through the recurrent combinations, where does that flow spend its time?

Structural centrality and flow centrality can disagree. An action can sit in many distinct combinations (structurally well-placed) while the combinations it sits in are rarely travelled (little flow). The instrument for the flow question is the random walk on hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights of Chitra & Raphael (2019), damped in the PageRank manner: from an action, the walk picks one of its recurrent combinations with probability proportional to the combination’s window count, then a member action with probability proportional to its occurrences inside that combination; with probability 0.15 it teleports to a uniformly random action. hypergraph_centrality(type = "pagerank") returns the stationary distribution of this walk.

One theoretical point makes the hypergraph version worth having: Chitra & Raphael prove that with edge-independent vertex weights the walk collapses to an ordinary PageRank on a weighted pairwise graph. The windowed construction is exactly the case that does not collapse — its incidence cells are within-window occurrence totals, which differ across combinations — so the scores below use information a pairwise reduction would destroy.

library(honets)
library(cograph)

The flow scores

The hypergraph is the same recurrent structure as in the previous tutorial: three-turn sliding windows, singletons removed, combinations kept when they recur in at least 50 windows.

hg <- window_hypergraph(human_long, action = "code",
                        actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp",
                        window = 3L, min_size = 2L, min_weight = 50L)
hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = "pagerank")
##        node   pagerank
## 1   Command 0.16951967
## 2   Correct 0.08046350
## 3 Frustrate 0.09197984
## 4   Inquire 0.07915760
## 5 Interrupt 0.07757647
## 6    Refine 0.07516957
## 7   Request 0.10603642
## 8   Specify 0.27454057
## 9    Verify 0.04555635

The walk spends 27% of its time on Specify and 17% on Command — together almost half of all flow on the two core directive actions. Request is third at 11%. At the other end, Verify receives 4.6%, barely above the teleportation floor: verification is visited, but the recurrent combinations that contain it carry little traffic. The window counts (hyperedge weights) and occurrence totals (vertex weights) are picked up from the hypergraph automatically; no further arguments are needed.

What recurrence adds to the ranking

Setting every combination’s weight to 1 removes the recurrence information while keeping the combination structure — the walk then treats a combination seen 722 times and one seen 50 times as equal.

hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = "pagerank", edge_weights = 1)
##        node   pagerank
## 1   Command 0.14355945
## 2   Correct 0.10068658
## 3 Frustrate 0.12215641
## 4   Inquire 0.10413195
## 5 Interrupt 0.07909551
## 6    Refine 0.08056093
## 7   Request 0.09455009
## 8   Specify 0.21278382
## 9    Verify 0.06247525

Two movements stand out against the recurrence-weighted scores above. Frustrate rises from 9.2% to 12.2% and Correct from 8.0% to 10.1%: these actions appear in many distinct combinations, so equal weighting favors them. Specify falls from 27.5% to 21.3%. The comparison separates two kinds of prominence — diversity of contexts (unit weights) versus volume of traffic (window counts) — and the default deliberately measures the latter.

Seeing the flow

splot(clique_expansion(hg), minimum = 0.05,
      title = "The co-membership structure the walk moves on")

Flow versus structure

The H-eigenvector scores the same hypergraph on presence alone: which actions sit in combinations whose other members are themselves central.

hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = c("H", "pagerank"), sort_by = "pagerank")
##        node         H   pagerank
## 1   Specify 0.4281911 0.27454057
## 2   Command 0.3773413 0.16951967
## 3   Request 0.3043738 0.10603642
## 4 Frustrate 0.3637328 0.09197984
## 5   Correct 0.3337657 0.08046350
## 6   Inquire 0.3340307 0.07915760
## 7 Interrupt 0.2831700 0.07757647
## 8    Refine 0.2820356 0.07516957
## 9    Verify 0.2580999 0.04555635

The table is ordered by PageRank, so reading down the H column shows where the two measures part company. They agree at the top (Specify, then Command) and at the bottom (Verify last) but disagree in the middle, and the disagreement is informative. H’s third-highest score goes to Frustrate (0.36), and it puts Correct and Inquire (0.33) above Request (0.30); PageRank reverses this, placing Request third (0.11) well above Correct and Inquire (0.08). The reason is the weight layer: Request sits inside the heaviest combinations in the data — Command, Request, Specify alone recurs 583 times — while Frustrate, Correct, and Inquire spread across many lighter ones. Structure says Frustrate is well-connected; flow says the traffic runs through Request.

Is the ranking an artifact of the damping choice?

Damping is the one free parameter, so the conclusion must survive changing it. Two calls bracket the default of 0.85.

hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = "pagerank", damping = 0.5)
##        node   pagerank
## 1   Command 0.14076338
## 2   Correct 0.09467131
## 3 Frustrate 0.10271757
## 4   Inquire 0.09384650
## 5 Interrupt 0.09208368
## 6    Refine 0.09143617
## 7   Request 0.10586887
## 8   Specify 0.20117920
## 9    Verify 0.07743333
hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = "pagerank", damping = 0.95)
##        node   pagerank
## 1   Command 0.17944634
## 2   Correct 0.07584459
## 3 Frustrate 0.08761813
## 4   Inquire 0.07451968
## 5 Interrupt 0.07335385
## 6    Refine 0.07001781
## 7   Request 0.10707234
## 8   Specify 0.29750537
## 9    Verify 0.03462188

The ordering of all nine actions is identical at damping 0.5, 0.85, and 0.95; only the spread changes. Less teleportation concentrates mass on the structure (Specify grows from 20.1% at 0.5 to 29.8% at 0.95, Verify shrinks from 7.7% to 3.5%), but no two actions trade places. The ranking can be reported without a damping caveat. In the undamped limit the scores converge to the walk’s stationary distribution — the pi column that [hypergraph_cluster()] reports, where Specify likewise holds 0.31.

When to use which

  • type = "pagerank" — the question is about flow or traffic: where activity concentrates, weighted by how often combinations recur. It uses both weight layers of a [window_hypergraph()], tolerates disconnected structure (teleportation), and its damping default can be reported without sensitivity caveats when the ranking is stable, as here.
  • type = "H" / "Z" — the question is about structural position in the combination pattern, deliberately ignoring recurrence. Divergence from PageRank is itself a finding: it locates actions whose prominence is contextual diversity rather than volume.
  • type = "clique" — a pairwise baseline (eigenvector centrality on the clique expansion); useful to check whether the hypergraph adds anything beyond a graph. When the incidence is binary, PageRank too collapses to a pairwise computation — the collapse theorem — so on binary hypergraphs prefer the cheaper graph method and reserve the hypergraph walk for genuinely edge-dependent weights.
  • pi from [hypergraph_cluster()] — the undamped stationary distribution; appropriate when the hypergraph is connected and no teleportation smoothing is wanted.

References

  • Benson, A. R. (2019). Three hypergraph eigenvector centralities. SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science, 1(2), 293–312.
  • Chitra, U., & Raphael, B. J. (2019). Random walks on hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights. ICML 2019, PMLR 97, 1172–1181.
  • Hayashi, K., Aksoy, S. G., Park, C. H., & Park, H. (2020). Hypergraph random walks, Laplacians, and clustering. CIKM 2020, 495–504.
